Financial planning · Balance sheet · Visual planning guide

Map your household net worth: assets, debts and financial resilience

Use a waterfall, an asset-composition chart and stress comparisons to understand what net worth measures and how liquidity and debt change the picture.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The central idea

Net worth measures assets less liabilities on a date. Cash flow and accessible reserves answer different questions about the household’s ability to meet payments.

01

Put every balance on the same date

A household balance sheet records what you own and what you owe. Net worth is assets − liabilities. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s financial-planning lesson explains this calculation using current values and distinguishes the balance sheet from the household budget.

Use a common observation date. Mixing an old home estimate, today’s investment statement and a debt balance from last year can create a misleading total. Record valuation uncertainty alongside assets that have no readily observable market price.

The default example lists a CAD 600,000 home, CAD 150,000 in market investments and CAD 30,000 in cash. Assets total CAD 780,000. Subtracting a CAD 350,000 mortgage and CAD 20,000 of other debts gives CAD 410,000 net worth. All figures are hypothetical and describe a simplified balance sheet.

02

Follow the bridge from gross assets to net worth

The waterfall adds each asset and subtracts each debt. The final navy bar is the net amount. Its endpoint can be negative: that means the listed liabilities exceed the listed asset values. A signed result is more informative than clipping the chart at zero.

Keep the home and mortgage treatment consistent. This chart lists gross home value as an asset and the mortgage as a liability. Alternatively, a presentation could show home equity alone. Adding home equity and then subtracting the mortgage again would count the debt twice.

Debt repayment and saving can affect the balance sheet in different ways. Paying principal with existing cash reduces cash and debt by the same amount, leaving net worth unchanged at that instant. Paying interest reduces cash without reducing principal. Future interest savings, fees, taxes and changes in asset values are separate effects rather than an immediate increase created by moving cash between rows.

03

Read composition alongside accessibility

The donut divides listed gross assets among the home, investments and cash. Its denominator is total listed assets before debt. It does not show an investment allocation, household spending shares or the fraction of net worth available to spend.

A home can dominate gross assets while supplying little immediate liquidity. Accessing its value may require selling, borrowing, paying costs or changing living arrangements. An investment account may be easier to sell but exposed to price movements, settlement timing, account restrictions or tax consequences.

Cash and deposits also need context: some may be committed to upcoming bills or a separate goal. Add a liquidity review alongside the net-worth total, listing which resources can meet which payments and when. The emergency-reserve tool starts from spending needs, rather than assuming that a positive balance sheet guarantees a sufficient cash buffer.

04

Watch the equity cushion change under stress

The grouped bars compare asset values with debts under separate home and investment declines, then both together. Cash and debt balances remain fixed in these instantaneous scenarios. A fall in a financed asset’s market value does not automatically reduce the amount owed.

In the default combined stress, home value falls 20% and investments fall 25%. Assets become CAD 622,500 while debts remain CAD 370,000. Net worth becomes CAD 252,500, a CAD 157,500 reduction, or about 38.4% of starting net worth. The percentage change in net worth can exceed the percentage change in gross assets because the liabilities remain.

The matrix expands this into combinations of home and market declines. Each signed cell reports resulting net worth in CAD. Gold negative cells mean debts exceed stressed assets. The selected stress percentages and matrix are alternative assumptions, with no probability attached and no forecast of property or investment prices.

05

Connect the snapshot to the rest of the plan

This simplified example omits pensions, businesses, other property, taxes triggered by sale, transaction costs and additional obligations. A more complete inventory can include those items with clear definitions. Be careful when combining amounts before and after tax or treating a future income entitlement as an immediately spendable lump sum.

A rise in net worth can come from saving, debt reduction, asset-price changes or new information about values. Track those drivers separately when comparing dates. An increase caused by a property revaluation does not necessarily improve the monthly budget; a change in interest costs can tighten cash flow without immediately changing principal balances.

Use the balance sheet with a cash-flow plan, emergency reserve and dated goals. Record the valuation date, sources and included obligations, then repeat on a consistent basis. The useful question is how the household’s resources support its commitments over time, rather than whether one headline number is above someone else’s.
